per_question.question: Lambda SnapStart and provisioned concurrency both exist to reduce cold-start latency, but you can't enable both on the same function version. Using what each mechanism actually does, explain why they're mutually exclusive and which runtimes get the free option.

per_question.generated_answer:
Lambda SnapStart and provisioned concurrency both aim to reduce cold-start latency, but they work in different ways and cannot be used together on the same function version.

Lambda SnapStart uses cached snapshots of the execution environment to improve startup performance, essentially bypassing the need to initialize the environment from scratch on every invocation. This is done at no additional cost for Java 11 and Java 17 runtimes.

Provisioned concurrency, on the other hand, pre-initializes a set number of execution environments ahead of time, making them ready to respond immediately to incoming function requests. This is useful for interactive workloads that are sensitive to latency.

The reason they're mutually exclusive is that provisioned concurrency requires the execution environment to be pre-initialized, which is exactly what SnapStart aims to avoid by caching snapshots. If both mechanisms were enabled, the cached snapshots would be overwritten by the pre-initialized environments, negating the benefits of both.

The free option, SnapStart, is available for Java 11 and Java 17 runtimes, while provisioned concurrency is available for all runtimes.

Provisioned concurrency reduces cold starts by keeping a specified number of execution environments pre-initialized and ready in advance. Because both are alternative solutions to the same cold-start problem, Lambda doesn't allow configuring them together on one function version. SnapStart is available at no extra cost for the Java 11 and Java 17 runtimes, while provisioned concurrency incurs additional charges regardless of runtime.
